Citi's 8,100 S&P 500 target requires both halves to perform, but NVIDIA's gains mask JPMorgan's 6% slide as the 10-year yield hits 5.22%.

Realty Income has dropped 11% since late August, but its 5.6% yield means any rate relief could spark a fast valuation recovery.

Hyperscaler capex could hit $800 billion in 2026, yet one top spender's free cash flow already turned negative $7.6 billion last quarter.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Microsoft didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat MSFT. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

Since August 28, Realty Income (NYSE:O) has fallen 10.91%. Over the same stretch, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) gained 4.15% and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) rose 5.38%.

Shutterstock

That split sits underneath the S&P 500 target of 8,100 from Scott Chronert, head of US equity strategy at Citi Research. This index target is a forecast about which half of the market stops falling.

Chronert laid out the condition himself: "We need both parts of the market performing. We need that AI influence component that we argue is just over half of the index as well as the other half. That's going to beat to a more traditional macro drummer."

The AI half has already risen, while the other half, priced off the cost of money, has slipped while the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.22%, so the target depends on rate relief as much as on earnings.

AI Stocks and Rate-Sensitive Stocks Are Moving in Opposite Directions

NVIDIA and Microsoft trade on AI capital spending, which lifted NVIDIA's data center revenue 117% last quarter. Banks, REITs, utilities and retailers trade on yields, because higher long rates raise borrowing costs and make dividends less competitive with Treasurys.

title: Should Microsoft Stock's New High Stop You From Buying?
detail:
Should Microsoft Stock's New High Stop You From Buying?
Trefis Team
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 1:19 PM CDT 3 min read
MSFT
Trade MSFT on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Most investors apply one rule to a stock like Microsoft (MSFT): buy low and never at the top. Microsoft stock closed near its 52-week high on October 13, 2026, making it the wrong time to buy under that logic. Rather than asking whether the price is too high, market participants should examine the historical performance of Microsoft's earlier highs. Does that rule hold for Microsoft?

Why Microsoft Stock Is At A High

Microsoft stock is at a high because the company earns more than it did a year ago. The share price rose 6.4% before dividends over the past year, while net income for the twelve months to June 2026 rose 31.3%.

Investors are actually paying less for that profit. The price-to-earnings multiple, which measures what investors pay for each dollar of profit, was 37.3 a year ago and is 30.2 now.

That growth is clearest in the cloud business. Revenue from Azure and other cloud services grew 43% in fiscal Q4 2026, the quarter to June. Management noted on that quarter's call that customer demand continues to exceed available capacity.

If you have held Microsoft for years, your biggest question may be taxes, not whether to buy at a high. See how a tax-aware transition works.

What Happened After Microsoft Stock's Earlier Highs?

Historical data answers the question of how often Microsoft stock rises in the year following a peak. Since October 2016, counting at most one high every six months, the stock has set 13 earlier 52-week highs with a full year after them. It was higher a year later after 12 of those instances.

The middle result was a gain of 31.1% a year later. A buyer purchasing Microsoft at a high usually experienced a strong following year rather than a trading mistake.

Is A High A Worse Time To Buy?

The data indicates otherwise for Microsoft. Buying on any trading day over the same years gave a middle gain of 30.2% a year later, just below the result after a high. The rule against buying at the top has not held for the company, making a high about as good a day to buy as any other.

What Should A Buyer At A High Expect?

Buyers usually face a small dip, but not always. The worst result came after the June 2025 high. A buyer at that time was 12.0% down a year later. That is why the rule is not foolish. Yet the June 2025 high was also the only one after which the stock closed 20% or more below the buying price within the year.

title: Not Microsoft. Not Alphabet. Here's the Cloud Giant I'm Most Bullish About.
detail:
Not Microsoft. Not Alphabet. Here's the Cloud Giant I'm Most Bullish About.
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 10:43 AM CDT 4 min read
GOOG
MSFT
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The cloud computing sector is one of the most interesting parts of the stock market right now. There are several companies spending more than $100 billion each to build and equip new data centers this year, and their capital expenditures are projected to rise once again in 2027. That's a ton of money being invested in this sector, but these companies wouldn't be doing it if they didn't see major potential.

The big three providers of cloud computing infrastructure are Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL). While Microsoft and Alphabet have exciting prospects, I'm far more bullish on Amazon for one reason: Amazon Web Services (AWS) has a bigger influence on its overall results than the cloud arms of Microsoft and Alphabet have on those companies. And it's easy to see why I'm so optimistic about it.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
AWS is seeing its growth accelerate

AWS is the biggest cloud computing service in the world, with a market share of about 28%. It was also the first to be launched. Although it looked to be falling behind the other two on artificial intelligence (AI) at the start of the AI race, Amazon has caught back up and established itself as a popular option for running AI workloads.

In its pursuit of that market, it has been spending more and more on cloud infrastructure, and it's on course for around $220 billion in data center capital expenditures this year. That leads the pack, but what returns on investment are shareholders seeing from those outlays?

During the second quarter, AWS revenue grew 37% year over year. For comparison, it grew 28% during the first quarter and 24% in 2025's fourth quarter. That's a strong acceleration for a business the size of AWS, so it's clearly seeing a strong return on investment.

However, investors also want to see these cloud segments turn a real profit, and that's what separates AWS from its peers.

AWS is a huge part of Amazon's business

During the second quarter, AWS' operating income surged 64% year over year, and this is what makes Amazon a better stock pick than Microsoft or Alphabet. The company may be best known for its massive e-commerce operation, but such businesses produce pretty slim operating margins. By contrast, the core business units of Microsoft and Alphabet are high-margin software and advertising businesses.
